summary: Describes the SASLprep profile of stringprep, for preparing Unicode user names and passwords for comparison, intended for use with SASL. It was replaced by RFC 7613.

plainLanguage.summary: Different keyboards can type the same word in different ways. This memo is a clean-up rule so a name or password looks the same everywhere. A newer document replaced it.

questions: how are unicode passwords normalized for sasl
subtitle: A recipe for cleaning up Unicode user names and passwords so they compare the same everywhere.

tldr.problem: Users around the world type user names and passwords in Unicode, and the same visible text can be encoded in different ways that would fail a naive comparison.
tldr.mechanism: SASLprep is a profile of the stringprep algorithm that maps some characters, normalizes with Unicode form KC, bans a list of unsuitable characters and checks bidirectional text.
tldr.outcome: It was published as a Standards Track document and later replaced by RFC 7613.

today: RFC 4013 is obsoleted by RFC 7613, which replaces this profile.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Simple user names and passwords are used everywhere on the Internet. To make input and comparison behave sensibly for people in different languages, RFC 4013 defines how to prepare internationalized user names and passwords for comparison. One algorithm serves both. It assumes strings are made of Unicode characters.

The document defines the SASLprep profile of stringprep (RFC 3454). It is meant for SASL mechanisms such as PLAIN, CRAM-MD5 and DIGEST-MD5.

It is not intended for identity strings that are not simple user names, such as email addresses, domain names or distinguished names, or for strings that need different handling such as case folding. It does not change any existing protocol; a specification must explicitly incorporate it.
sections.plainLanguage: Different people might type the same name with different hidden characters. This memo says how to tidy a name or password first so the computer sees them as equal.

sections.title: The SASLprep Steps
sections.content:
The profile uses Unicode 3.2 and has four parts. Mapping: non-ASCII space characters are mapped to SPACE (U+0020), and the characters stringprep table B.1 lists as commonly mapped to nothing are removed. Normalization: Unicode normalization form KC is used. Prohibited output: a list of character classes is rejected. Bidirectional characters: strings are checked as described in section 6 of stringprep.

Unassigned code points are those in stringprep table A.1.
sections.plainLanguage: First swap odd spaces for normal ones and drop invisible bits. Then write letters in one standard way. Then throw out anything not allowed.

sections.title: What Is Prohibited
sections.content: The profile prohibits these classes from stringprep: non-ASCII space characters, ASCII control characters, non-ASCII control characters, private use characters, non-character code points, surrogate code points, characters inappropriate for plain text, characters inappropriate for canonical representation, characters that change display properties or are deprecated, and tagging characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters are like invisible ink or secret controls. The rules ban them from names and passwords.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content: The RFC gives seven examples. A soft hyphen between I and X is mapped to nothing, giving IX. Plain user is unchanged, and USER keeps its case so it will not match it. The character U+00AA becomes a, and U+2168 becomes IX, matching the first example. A control character U+0007 is an error because it is prohibited, and U+0627 followed by U+0031 is an error from the bidirectional check.
sections.plainLanguage: Fancy versions of a letter turn into the plain one, invisible bits vanish, and forbidden things cause an error. Capital letters stay capital.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The output is designed to be canonical and well-formed. However, because of an anomaly in the specification of Unicode normalization, canonical equivalence is not guaranteed for a select few character sequences that do not appear in well-formed text. The RFC was published despite this known problem and expected a revision before further progress on the Standards Track.

Preparation may affect brute force and dictionary attacks. The number of possible prepared strings is lower than for all Unicode strings, but the number of usable names and passwords is greater than with ASCII only. User names and passwords should be protected from eavesdropping. The profile is not for identity strings needing other handling, and the IANA section records that SASLprep was registered as the first version of the profile in the stringprep registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The clean-up rule has one tiny known gap for strange text. Names and passwords still need to be kept away from snoopers.
